--------
Charleston White joins VladTV for a blunt conversation about the fatal shooting of Chicago rapper BloodHound Q50 and why he believes Q50 knew he was about to die. Vlad reflects on warning Q50 to leave Chicago after BloodHound Lil Jeff’s murder, comparing the pattern to past interviews with FBG Duck and Mo3 amid conflicts involving Yella Beezy. White connects Q50’s mindset to figures like Tupac and King Von, arguing that many young men caught in street life expect an early death. The discussion also turns to BloodHound Poo Man being killed after the funeral, the cycle of retaliation in Chicago, hip hop’s “gangster image,” and how music, violence, and legal outcomes influence street culture. White also references Lil Durk, DJ Akademiks, and courtroom precedent in a wider debate on accountability, survival, and the realities facing young artists.

--------
In this VladTV interview, Rex Holloway reflects on leaving the Aryan Brotherhood at 22 while still facing five more years in prison. He explains why the move was strategic, how AB members reacted, and why studying the stock market, economics, and history pushed him toward a different future. Holloway also details holding rank across multiple prison units before deciding gang life no longer made sense.

The conversation turns to the brutal reality of solitary confinement, including Holloway’s six and a half years in administrative segregation at Ferguson Unit in East Texas. He describes extreme heat, tiny cells, limited recreation, riots, gas exposure, and the long-term effects of isolation, including post incarceration syndrome. Vlad also references former Mafia captain Michael Franzese’s comments on solitary, connecting broader conversations about prison reform, mental health, prison gangs, Aryan Circle, ABT, and life after incarceration.

Part 1: https://youtu.be/U21AbA_cZII
--------
Former Delta Force operator Dale Comstock joins Vlad to revisit the aftermath of the U.S. invasion of Panama in December 1989 and the hunt for Manuel Noriega during Operation Just Cause. Comstock describes living out of helicopters while chasing intelligence leads across Panama, staking out downtown Panama City near the Vatican Embassy, and later learning that Noriega’s security team had prepared explosives at a villa packed with millions of dollars.  

The conversation follows Noriega’s arrest, transfer to Miami, conviction on drug trafficking, racketeering and money laundering charges, his later extradition to France, return to Panama, imprisonment and death in 2017 after complications from brain tumor surgery. Comstock reflects on Noriega as a corrupt strongman and drug-linked ruler, but contrasts him with Saddam Hussein and his sons, whom he describes as far more evil. A blunt discussion on power, justice, U.S. intervention and America’s role in confronting dictators.

--------
Ramon “Mundo” Mendoza revisits the fallout surrounding the 1992 film *American Me* in this VladTV interview, explaining why one scene involving Edward James Olmos’ Santana character—widely linked to Cheyenne Cadena—angered figures tied to the Mexican Mafia. Mendoza compares the film’s prison-gang realism to *Blood In Blood Out*, praises its depiction of mannerisms, and discusses his law enforcement screening in Orange, California. He also addresses long-running claims about killings connected to the movie, saying he personally knew Charlie Brown Manriquez and Rocky “Manuel” Luna, and knew the story of Ana Lizarraga. Mendoza recalls meeting Olmos at Colima Restaurant in downtown Los Angeles with technical advisor Tony Casas, assessing rumored threats, extortion concerns, and the role of the controversial juvenile hall rape scene. Danny Trejo, Benjamin Bratt, Folsom Prison, Big Hazard, and *60 Minutes* also come up in this detailed account.

--------
In this VladTV interview, Rex Holloway explains the turning point that led him to walk away from the Aryan Brotherhood at age 22. From Texas prison units like Torres, Ferguson, and East Ham, Holloway describes growing disillusioned with prison politics, weak leadership, and the reality of life in solitary confinement. He recalls reading about John Gotti, Paul Castellano, and Sammy “The Bull” Gravano’s *Underboss*, which changed how he viewed loyalty and trust in organized crime.

The conversation centers on a botched prison hit involving poison-laced tacos, a written kite, and a chain of mistakes involving Wizard, Dirty Joe, and a man nicknamed Iceman. As the conspiracy unraveled, Holloway says he realized he could spend life in prison over “sloppy” decisions and chose to quit before the fallout hit. A rare firsthand look at gang life, prison hierarchy, and leaving extremism behind.
